title: Why People Behave the Way They Do
question: How much of what people do at work is explained by the situations, incentives and social expectations leaders create — and how should that change the way you design them?

overview.text: Week 1 examined how individuals think. This week examines why people act as they do in groups and organizations, and how leaders shape that behavior — often unintentionally. The central claim is uncomfortable for anyone who manages people: behavior that looks like a character flaw is frequently a reasonable response to a situation, an incentive or a norm that someone else designed. The corollary is just as uncomfortable: the famous studies used to make that claim have a mixed replication record, and you need to know which ones to trust.

The four lessons move from the person to the system. Lesson 1 examines situational power — conformity, attribution and the replication audit of classic social psychology. Lesson 2 examines motivation: self-determination theory, when rewards undermine intrinsic interest, and the evidence that intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance. Lesson 3 turns to the economics of incentives: principal–agent problems, the multitask model, metric decay and gaming, with a documented banking example. Lesson 4 examines the social economy of work: reciprocity, norms, fairness, status and psychological safety.

You will practise the ideas three ways. In the Incentive Designer you build an incentive system for a fictional hospital unit and watch effort, gaming, cooperation and motivation trade off. The case puts you inside a fictional payments company whose growth metric has started to decay under pay pressure. The assignment asks you to diagnose incentive misalignments in a fictional professional baseball organization and propose redesigns, with honest predictions about the new problems each redesign will create.

objectives: Diagnose a recurring behavior problem by examining incentives, norms, status and friction before attributing it to individual character.
Classify influential social-psychology findings as robust, context-dependent or failed to replicate, and explain what that implies for using them.
Explain self-determination theory and the conditions under which rewards strengthen or undermine motivation.
Apply the principal–agent and multitask models to predict effort diversion and gaming under a proposed incentive.
Design an incentive system that integrates measure, unit, horizon, payout shape, monitoring and non-financial levers, and state its expected side effects.
Evaluate claims about reciprocity, fairness and psychological safety by distinguishing correlational from causal evidence.

lessons.title: The Power of the Situation — and What Survived Replication
lessons.summary: Behavior is jointly produced by people and the situations they are placed in, and the classic social-psychology evidence for situational power is a mix of robust, fragile and failed findings.
objectives: Explain why observers over-attribute behavior to character and under-attribute it to situations, and what that means for diagnosing performance problems.
Describe what the meta-analytic evidence on conformity does and does not show.
Classify a famous social-psychology finding as robust, context-dependent or failed to replicate, and justify the classification.
lessons.executive: When someone behaves badly at work, the first explanation offered is usually about the person: lazy, political, uncoachable. Social psychology’s most durable lesson is that situations — what is rewarded, who is watching, what the group is doing — explain more behavior than observers expect. But the field’s own evidence is uneven. Conformity to unanimous groups is robust though variable. Ego depletion, once a staple of leadership books, failed a large preregistered test, and a systematic replication project found that published social-psychology effects were often smaller or less reliable than reported. Diagnose the situation first, and ask how well the study you are quoting has held up.

explore.text: Imagine three units in a large hospital system that all post poor hand-hygiene audit results in the same quarter. The chief nursing officer’s first instinct is to identify the careless nurses and retrain them. Before reading on, notice the assumption in that instinct: that the cause lives inside individual people. Now add three facts. In the first unit, the sanitizer dispensers are at the far end of each room. In the second, a respected senior physician routinely skips hand hygiene and nobody comments. In the third, audits are announced in advance everywhere except on night shift. Each fact is a feature of the situation, and each predicts the pattern of failures better than any personality inventory would. This is a hypothetical composite, but the pattern will be familiar to anyone who has investigated a quality problem.

Think of the last time someone in your organization was labelled “not a team player” or “not coachable.” Write down one feature of their situation — what they were measured on, who they reported to, what their peers were doing — that could have produced the same behavior in most people.

This lesson asks two questions that every executive needs to hold together. First, how much of behavior is explained by the situation rather than the person? Second, how much should you trust the famous studies that answer the first question? Social psychology built its public reputation on dramatic demonstrations of situational power. Over the last fifteen years, the field has also become a leader in auditing itself, and the audit produced uncomfortable results. You need both the insight and the audit.

understand.text: Persons, situations and the observer’s bias

Behavior is always produced by a person in a situation. The useful question is rarely “person or situation?” but “which features of the situation are doing the work, and for whom?” Observers, however, are systematically lopsided. Social psychologists use the term *fundamental attribution error* (also called correspondence bias) for the tendency to explain other people’s behavior by their dispositions — character, ability, attitude — while underweighting the pressures acting on them. The term is standard; how universal and how large the tendency is has been debated. Treat it as a reliable default, not a law.

The lopsidedness has a practical structure. When *you* miss a deadline, you see the competing demands, the late data and the unclear brief. When a colleague misses one, you see the colleague. Situational forces are often invisible to outsiders: incentives, informal norms, who is in the room, what happened last time someone raised a concern. The executive implication is direct. A performance problem that recurs across different people in the same role is evidence about the role.

understand.text: Conformity: robust, but variable

The most studied demonstration of situational power is Solomon Asch’s line-judgment task. A participant sits with a group of confederates who, on some trials, unanimously give an obviously wrong answer about which of several lines matches a reference line. Many participants go along with the group on at least some trials. Bond and Smith’s meta-analysis of studies using Asch’s task found that conformity is a real and repeatable phenomenon, but that its size varies: it rises with the size of the majority, is larger in more collectivist cultures, and declined in U.S. samples over the decades after Asch’s original work.

That combination — real but variable — is what most robust social findings look like. The direction generalizes: people shift toward unanimous groups, especially when they care about belonging to the group. The rate does not generalize: it depends on culture, era, stakes and how ambiguous the judgment is. In organizations, judgments are usually far more ambiguous than the length of a line, which plausibly makes social influence stronger, while dissent can also be rewarded, which makes it weaker. Because the size of the effect depends on the setting, the practical response is structural rather than exhortative: design meetings so that independent views are recorded before discussion.

blocks.text: A finding *replicates* when a new study, using the same procedure on new participants, produces a similar result. A *direct* replication repeats the method as closely as possible; a *conceptual* replication tests the same idea with a different method. Direct replications are the stronger test of whether the original result was reliable, because conceptual replications can succeed for different reasons or quietly go unpublished when they fail.

Why would a published result fail to replicate? The most common reasons are small samples (which produce noisy estimates), flexibility in analysis (testing several outcomes or exclusion rules and reporting the one that worked), and publication filters (journals preferring significant results). None requires fraud. Together they produce a literature in which published effects are, on average, larger than the true effects. Week 4 develops this formally; for now, the point is that a famous result is not the same as a reliable one.

understand.text: The replication record

In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration reported the results of repeating 100 studies from three leading psychology journals with high-powered designs and, where possible, the original materials. Most originals had reported statistically significant results; far fewer replications did, and the replication effect sizes averaged roughly half of the original estimates. Social psychology studies replicated less often than cognitive psychology studies. Originals with larger effects and stronger statistical evidence were more likely to hold up.

Ego depletion is the clearest cautionary tale for managers. The idea — that self-control draws on a limited resource that is used up by earlier acts of self-control — spread widely into leadership and productivity advice. A registered replication report in which more than twenty laboratories ran one preregistered protocol found a pooled effect close to zero.

challenge.text: The replication debate is not settled in every detail. Critics of the 2015 project argued that some replications differed from the originals in population or procedure, and that a single replication cannot establish that an effect is false. Proponents of ego depletion argued that the multi-lab protocol used too weak a manipulation. These objections deserve a hearing. But they cut both ways: if an effect appears only under narrow conditions that its proponents cannot specify in advance, it is not a reliable basis for designing organizations. The stronger, more general conclusion — published effects are often inflated and some celebrated ones are not real — has held across later many-laboratory projects.

There is also a mirror-image error. Having learned that situations matter, some leaders conclude that individual differences do not. That overcorrects. Ability, conscientiousness and expertise predict performance in many jobs, and selection decisions rest on that fact. Situations also select people: a sales floor with aggressive targets attracts and retains people comfortable with them. The mature position is interactional: people differ, situations differ, and the same incentive or norm produces different behavior in different people. Diagnosing the situation first is a sequencing rule, not a denial of character.

Finally, notice how social influence bears on the replication story itself. Findings became famous partly because they were surprising and partly because many people repeated them — textbooks, consultants and speakers citing each other. Popularity is a social signal, not an evidential one. The same conformity pressures that shape behavior in a meeting shape what a profession “knows.”

challenge.title: Methodological note: why surprising, small-sample findings are fragile

blocks.text: Suppose a true effect is small and a study is small. Only estimates that happen to come out large will clear the significance threshold, so the published estimate is biased upward even when every step was honest. A replication with a larger sample then lands closer to the true, smaller effect and is called a “failure.” This is why the 2015 project’s finding that stronger original evidence predicted replication matters: the size of the original p-value and sample are themselves information. When you read a classic study, ask how many participants it had, whether the analysis was specified in advance, and whether an independent multi-site test exists. Week 4’s Evidence Lab lets you simulate exactly this mechanism.

A second subtlety is the difference between an effect that is *zero* and one that is *unreliable*. A preregistered multi-lab null result for ego depletion is strong evidence that the standard paradigm does not produce a meaningful effect. It is weaker evidence about every possible version of self-control fatigue. Executives rarely need that philosophical precision; they need to know that the confident popular version has no reliable support.

apply.text: Consider a hypothetical government benefits agency where claim-processing errors are concentrated among newer staff. The director proposes a stricter hiring screen. A situational diagnosis asks first what newer staff are measured on (throughput targets that experienced staff have learned to negotiate), who sits near them (whether experienced colleagues are co-located or remote), and what happens when a new hire asks a question (whether supervisors treat it as a sign of weakness). If those features explain the pattern, a hiring screen will change the people and leave the error rate where it is.

In a hypothetical consulting firm, junior analysts rarely contradict partners’ hypotheses in client workshops, and several engagements later turn out to have been built on a wrong premise. The partners read this as a lack of confidence in the analysts. The conformity evidence suggests a structural fix: ask every participant to submit an independent estimate or recommendation in writing before discussion, and have the most senior person speak last. Those changes do not require anyone to become braver.

In player development, the same logic applies to evaluation meetings. If a group of coaches and analysts discusses a prospect after hearing the most senior evaluator’s view, the later views will drift toward it — not because the others lack conviction but because the meeting is structured to produce conformity. Recording independent grades before discussion, and rotating who speaks first, are cheap situational changes. Likewise, when a coach is described as “resistant to data,” ask what the coach is evaluated on, whether using the new information has ever been rewarded, and what happened the last time a coach publicly changed course.

apply.title: Executive twist: when you do not know whether it is the person or the role

blocks.text: You inherit a unit where one manager has had three direct reports quit in a year. You have exit interviews that are polite and vague, and the manager’s numbers are strong. You cannot run an experiment. A defensible approach treats the question as a comparison: how do turnover and engagement in this unit compare with similar units under different managers, and with this manager’s previous team? Is the manager’s span, workload or target different? If the pattern follows the manager across roles, the evidence points toward the person; if it follows the role across managers, toward the situation. You will rarely get a clean answer, so decide what information would change your mind before you look.

retain.text: Behavior is produced by people in situations, and observers systematically underweight the situation. Conformity to groups is a robust finding whose size varies with culture, era and stakes. The replication record of social psychology is mixed: some classics hold, many effects are smaller than published, and some popular claims such as ego depletion failed rigorous tests. Diagnose the role before the person, and check the evidence before quoting the study.

lessons.title: Why People Try: Self-Determination, Rewards and Crowding Out
lessons.summary: Motivation differs in kind as well as amount, and rewards can strengthen or weaken it depending on whether they feel controlling or informative and on what the work actually requires.
objectives: Explain self-determination theory’s distinction between autonomous and controlled motivation and its three proposed needs.
State the conditions under which rewards have been found to undermine intrinsic motivation, and the conditions under which they have not.
Use the evidence that intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance to decide what part of a job should carry a direct incentive.
lessons.executive: Two claims dominate popular writing on motivation: “pay people for what you want” and “money destroys intrinsic motivation.” Both are half right. Self-determination theory distinguishes autonomous from controlled motivation and argues that autonomy, competence and relatedness sustain the former. A large meta-analysis of experiments found that expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing an interesting task reduce later voluntary engagement, while informative positive feedback does not. A forty-year meta-analysis of performance found that intrinsic motivation and incentives both predict performance — intrinsic motivation more for quality, incentives more for quantity. The design question is which part of a job each should carry.

explore.text: A group of day-care centers has a problem: some parents arrive late to collect their children, and a teacher has to stay behind. Management introduces a modest fine for late pickup. Before reading on, predict what happens to the number of late pickups. Most people predict a decline. In the field experiment that Gneezy, Meier and Rey-Biel discuss, conducted in Israeli day-care centers, the number of late pickups rose after the fine was introduced — and stayed high after the fine was removed.
Write one sentence explaining why a fine might increase the behavior it was meant to reduce. Then write one sentence explaining why removing the fine did not restore the old behavior.

The standard economic prediction treated the fine as a price increase on lateness. What the fine also did was change what lateness meant. Before, being late was imposing on a teacher who stayed out of goodwill; afterwards, it was a service one could buy, at a price lower than many parents expected the guilt to cost. The fine supplied a new frame, and the old frame did not return when the price disappeared. This lesson is about that second channel: what incentives communicate, and how they interact with the reasons people already have for doing their work.

understand.text: Motivation differs in kind

Self-determination theory, developed by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, argues that the most important distinction is not how much motivation a person has but what kind. *Autonomous* motivation comes from interest in the activity or from having internalized its value; *controlled* motivation comes from pressure — rewards, punishments, guilt or the wish to look good. The theory proposes three basic psychological needs whose support fosters autonomous motivation: *autonomy* (feeling that one’s actions are self-endorsed), *competence* (feeling effective) and *relatedness* (feeling connected to others).

Importantly, the theory does not treat extrinsic motivation as uniformly bad. It describes a continuum of regulation: external (doing it for the reward or to avoid punishment), introjected (doing it to avoid guilt or protect self-esteem), identified (doing it because one values the outcome) and integrated (the value has become part of who one is). Extrinsically motivated work can become autonomous when people understand and endorse its purpose. A compliance officer may not find documentation interesting, yet can perform it autonomously because she values what it protects.

understand.text: When rewards undermine — and when they do not

Deci, Koestner and Ryan’s meta-analysis of 128 experiments tested whether rewards reduce people’s later, freely chosen engagement with an interesting task. The answer depended on the reward. Expected, tangible rewards made contingent on doing, completing or performing well at the task reduced free-choice intrinsic motivation. Positive verbal feedback tended to enhance it. The authors explain the pattern through cognitive evaluation theory, a part of self-determination theory: a reward that is experienced as *controlling* reduces felt autonomy, while one experienced as *informational* — telling people they are competent — does not.

understand.text: The day-care case shows a related but distinct mechanism that economists call *motivation crowding out*. Gneezy, Meier and Rey-Biel argue that incentives have two effects at once: the direct price effect predicted by standard economics, and a psychological effect on how people interpret the task and what their behavior signals. When the second runs opposite to the first and is larger, incentives backfire. Payments can also weaken the image value of doing good — volunteering looks less virtuous if it is paid — and can teach people that a task must be unpleasant if someone pays for it.
Jointly, not instead

If the story ended there, managers might conclude that incentives should be avoided. Cerasoli, Nicklin and Ford’s meta-analysis of 183 samples across school, work and physical domains, with more than 200,000 participants, tells a more useful story. Intrinsic motivation predicted performance with medium to strong correlations and remained predictive when incentives were present. The salience of the incentive mattered: when incentives were directly tied to performance, intrinsic motivation was a weaker predictor; when incentives were only indirectly tied, it was stronger. The authors also report that intrinsic motivation was more closely related to the quality of performance and incentives to its quantity.

challenge.text: The undermining effect has been contested for decades. Cameron, Pierce and colleagues argued in their own meta-analyses that the negative effects of reward were narrow and often absent, and that verbal rewards and rewards for meeting performance standards could increase interest. Deci, Koestner and Ryan responded that the earlier analyses had miscoded studies and combined conditions that should be separated. The forty-year meta-analysis by Cerasoli and colleagues partly reconciles the camps: incentives and intrinsic motivation both matter for performance, while direct, salient incentives change how much the intrinsic part contributes.

Three limits deserve emphasis. First, most undermining experiments measure minutes of voluntary play with a puzzle after a short session, not sustained work performance. The mechanism is credible; the size of the effect in a salaried job is unknown. Second, almost all paid work already involves expected, contingent pay. The relevant question is rarely whether to pay but how *salient* and how *tightly coupled* to specific outputs a payment should be. Third, crowding out can run in reverse — *crowding in* — when an incentive is read as recognition of competence or as evidence that the organization values the work.

There is also a selection effect that motivational theories often omit. Strong pay-for-output systems attract people who like them and repel people who do not. An organization that adds tight incentives may raise output partly by changing who works there, which can be good or bad depending on what the unmeasured part of the job requires. Weeks 7 and 8 return to this through the economics of contracts and organizational design.

challenge.title: Methodological note: correlations, salience and what a meta-analysis can tell you

blocks.text: Much of the evidence in a performance meta-analysis is correlational: people who report more interest also perform better. That pattern is compatible with interest causing performance, performance causing interest (doing well is enjoyable), or a third factor such as ability causing both. Moderator findings — like the role of incentive salience — compare studies rather than randomly assigning salience, so they share the same limitation. The experimental undermining literature has the opposite profile: strong causal identification in artificial settings. Neither alone answers a compensation committee’s question. Together they justify a cautious claim: the way incentives are framed and coupled to output plausibly changes how much intrinsic motivation contributes, and the effect is large enough to deserve design attention.

apply.text: Hypothetical: a teaching hospital considers paying residents a bonus for each completed discharge summary to reduce backlog. The task is mostly volume and low in interest, which suggests direct incentives will raise output. But summaries also carry quality that matters to the next clinician, and residents care about being seen as good doctors. A design informed by this lesson might pay a modest team-level bonus for backlog reduction, combined with audited quality feedback delivered as information about competence, rather than a per-document piece rate.

Hypothetical: an open-source software foundation wants more code reviews from volunteer contributors and proposes paying per review. The crowding-out evidence warns that payment may change what reviewing means — from contribution to a community to low-paid gig work — and may reduce reviews by people who were doing them for reputation. Alternatives include public recognition tied to review quality, faster merge rights for active reviewers (an autonomy and competence signal), and funding a small number of paid maintainers whose role is explicitly distinct from volunteering.

In player development, most players and staff are highly intrinsically motivated about the core craft. Self-determination theory suggests that development plans players help design (autonomy), with feedback framed as information about progress (competence) and delivered within trusted relationships (relatedness), are more likely to produce internalized commitment than plans imposed with tightly coupled rewards. That does not make incentives irrelevant: tasks low in interest and high in volume, such as completing routine data entry or recovery protocols, may respond well to simple, visible accountability. The design skill is to match the instrument to the task.

apply.title: Prerequisite: reading a correlation coefficient in a meta-analysis

blocks.text: Meta-analyses of field studies usually report a corrected correlation, written ρ (rho), between two variables across many samples. A ρ of .20 is conventionally described as modest and .40 as substantial for behavioral research, though such labels are rough. Squaring ρ gives the share of variance in one variable statistically associated with the other: ρ = .40 corresponds to 16 percent. That sounds small, but in a large organization a predictor associated with 16 percent of the variance in performance is very valuable. Remember that a correlation, even a meta-analytic one, does not establish which variable causes the other.

retain.text: Motivation differs in kind: autonomous motivation is sustained by support for autonomy, competence and relatedness. Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing an interesting task can undermine later voluntary engagement, while informative feedback does not. Incentives can change what a task means, as in the day-care fine. Yet intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance; the design question is how salient and tightly coupled incentives should be for each part of the work.
What feature of a reward makes it more likely to undermine intrinsic motivation, according to cognitive evaluation theory?
Explain the day-care result using the two effects of an incentive described by Gneezy and colleagues.

Expected, tangible, task-contingent rewards can undermine later free-choice interest; informative feedback tends not to.
Incentives carry meaning; a price can replace a norm and the norm may not return.
Intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance — the first more for quality, the second more for quantity.
Ask how salient and how tightly coupled to output an incentive should be, not simply whether to pay.

lessons.title: Rewarding A, Hoping for B: Agency, Multitasking and Gaming
lessons.summary: When people do several tasks that differ in how well they can be measured, strong incentives on the measured ones pull effort away from the rest and invite gaming, so incentive strength, metric choice and job design must be decided together.
objectives: Define the principal–agent problem and explain why information asymmetry makes incentive design necessary and difficult.
Apply the multitask model to predict where effort will move when one task is rewarded more strongly than others.
Distinguish effort on a measure, gaming of a measure and fraud, and identify design features that make gaming more likely.
Evaluate payout shape, horizon and monitoring as levers in an incentive system.
lessons.executive: Every incentive system pays for a measure, and every measure is an imperfect proxy for what the organization actually wants. The principal–agent lens explains why you need incentives: you cannot observe effort directly. The multitask model explains why strong incentives can make things worse: effort flows toward what is measured and away from what is not. Kerr’s classic essay collects the predictable result — organizations rewarding A while hoping for B. The Wells Fargo enforcement action shows the extreme case: volume targets and incentive pay accompanied by accounts opened without customer consent. Choose measures, horizons, payout shapes and monitoring as one system, and ask what a rational person would do if paid exactly this way.

explore.text: In September 2016 the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau announced a $100 million penalty against Wells Fargo Bank. The bureau stated that employees, working under sales targets and incentive-compensation programs, had opened deposit and credit-card accounts without customers’ knowledge or consent, and it ordered remediation. The bank was not short of codes of conduct, and most of its employees presumably did not set out to deceive anyone. Something about the system made a large number of people behave in ways that harmed customers and, eventually, the bank itself.

Before reading on, list three features of a sales-incentive system that would make unauthorized account openings more likely. Then list one feature that would make them less likely without abandoning sales goals.

It is tempting to treat such episodes as moral failures by bad actors. Some were. But the more useful question for a leader is structural: what did the system pay for, what could it observe, and what would a reasonable person under pressure do? This lesson gives you three tools for answering it — the principal–agent problem, the multitask model and the diagnostic habit of comparing what is rewarded with what is hoped for.

understand.text: The principal–agent problem

A *principal* (an owner, a manager, a public) delegates work to an *agent* (an employee, a contractor, an official) whose actions the principal cannot fully observe and whose interests do not perfectly coincide with the principal’s. Two frictions follow. *Hidden action* (moral hazard): the principal sees outcomes but not effort, and outcomes are affected by luck. *Hidden information* (adverse selection): the agent knows things — about their ability, the client, the difficulty of the task — that the principal does not. Incentive pay is a response to hidden action: if you cannot see effort, pay for something correlated with it. The cost is that pay now depends on noise and on whatever the measure misses.

blocks.text: Economists describe incentives by their *power*: how much an agent’s pay changes when a measured output changes. A piece rate or uncapped commission is high-powered; a fixed salary is low-powered. High-powered incentives sharpen effort on the measure but transfer risk to the agent (whose pay now varies with luck) and magnify any gap between the measure and the goal. Most real compensation mixes a low-powered base with a higher-powered component, plus promotion and reputation, which are themselves powerful incentives even when no bonus exists.

understand.text: The multitask problem

Holmström and Milgrom’s multitask model formalizes what goes wrong when agents divide effort among tasks that differ in how well they can be measured. If one task is measured precisely and another poorly, a strong incentive on the first pulls effort away from the second. When the poorly measured task matters, the optimal response may be to *weaken* incentives on the measured task, pay a salary, or redesign the job so that tasks with similar measurability are grouped together. The model explains why many professionals are paid salaries rather than piece rates, and why job design and asset ownership are incentive instruments in their own right.

understand.text: Rewarding A while hoping for B

Steven Kerr’s essay assembled examples from government, war, medicine, universities, sport and business in which organizations rewarded one behavior while hoping for another — rewarding individual statistics while hoping for teamwork, rewarding grant volume while hoping for teaching, rewarding visible activity while hoping for results. Kerr traced the problem to a fascination with objective, easily counted criteria and a reluctance to reward behavior that is hard to observe. It is a practitioner essay built on illustrations, not a systematic study, but its diagnostic question has lasted because it works: what does the system actually pay for?

A related idea is usually stated as an aphorism. *Goodhart’s law*, in the popular wording “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure,” and *Campbell’s law*, that quantitative social indicators used for decisions become subject to corruption pressure, both describe the same mechanism. A measure is chosen because, before anyone was paid on it, it correlated with the goal. Once pay depends on it, people find cheaper ways to move the measure than to move the goal, and the correlation weakens. Treat these as heuristics with broad practical support rather than as laws with known effect sizes.

challenge.text: The opposite conclusion — “incentives don’t work” — is just as wrong. Incentives change behavior; that is precisely why they are dangerous when poorly designed. The forty-year meta-analysis discussed in the previous lesson found incentives related to the quantity of performance, and the multitask model assumes, realistically, that agents respond to what is paid. Gaming is the predictable side effect of an incentive that works on the wrong measure, not evidence that incentives fail. The executive judgment is about where to set power, not whether to have it.

A second objection is that agents are not only maximizing pay. People care about fairness, identity and how they are seen, and incentives can change those motives too. Gneezy, Meier and Rey-Biel argue that incentives send signals — about what the principal expects, what the task is worth and whether the agent is trusted — that can strengthen or weaken behavior beyond the direct price effect. A heavily monitored, high-powered scheme can tell employees they are not trusted, and some respond by doing exactly what is paid and nothing more.

A third limit concerns blame. Systemic explanations can become an excuse. Regulators in the Wells Fargo matter held the institution accountable, and individuals who falsified records made choices. The lesson for leaders is not that individuals bear no responsibility but that a system that reliably produces misconduct across many people is a leadership failure, whatever else it is. Week 13 returns to accountability and governance.

challenge.title: Methodological note: the informativeness principle and why noise matters

blocks.text: Agency theory implies that an incentive should be based on measures that are informative about the agent’s effort — that is, which change when effort changes and change little otherwise. Measures dominated by luck impose risk on the agent without improving effort, and risk-averse agents demand compensation for bearing it. One implication is *relative performance evaluation*: comparing an agent with peers who face the same shocks filters out common luck. The cost is that it turns colleagues into rivals and can reduce cooperation. Another implication is that adding a noisy but independent measure can be valuable even if it is imperfect. In practice, leaders rarely compute any of this, but the questions transfer: what moves this measure besides effort, and what does using it do to cooperation?

apply.text: Hypothetical: a city government sets an emergency-department target that patients be seen within a fixed time after arrival. Effort rises; waiting times fall. But some hospitals start the clock later, hold ambulances outside, or re-label areas so that patients count as “seen” sooner. The multitask lens predicts this: the measured dimension (time to first contact) is a weak proxy for the goal (timely, appropriate care), and staff have many other tasks. Responses include auditing how the clock is started, pairing the target with outcome measures, and leaving room for clinical judgment rather than raising the bonus.

Hypothetical: an investment bank pays analysts on the number of deals they help close each quarter. Analysts begin pushing marginal deals forward to the end of the quarter and spend less time on research that would kill bad deals early. A redesign might pay on deal quality over a longer horizon, defer part of the bonus, and protect a review role whose job is to say no.

In baseball operations, the same logic applies to scouts evaluated on how many of their signed players reach a given level, coaches evaluated on short-term statistical improvement, or analysts evaluated on the number of reports produced. Each measure correlates with something the organization wants and each can be moved cheaply: signing safer, lower-ceiling players; emphasizing changes that show up quickly in statistics over slower foundational work; producing reports nobody reads. The week’s assignment asks you to trace such misalignments through a fictional organization and design around them.

apply.title: Executive twist: the numbers are excellent and you are uneasy

blocks.text: Your highest-performing team has beaten its target four quarters running. Two former team members, in exit interviews, hint that “everyone knows how the numbers are made.” Nothing specific has been alleged. Investigating signals distrust to your best performers and may find nothing; not investigating risks a much larger problem later. A proportionate response is to audit the measure rather than the people: sample transactions for verification, compare the team’s patterns (timing, reversals, customer complaints) with peers, and make the review routine across all teams so that it is not an accusation. Decide in advance what pattern would prompt a deeper inquiry.

retain.text: Incentives exist because principals cannot observe effort, and they are dangerous because every measure is an imperfect proxy. When agents have several tasks of differing measurability, strong incentives on the measured ones divert effort from the rest; sometimes the right answer is weaker incentives or a redesigned job. Measures decay under pressure as people find cheap ways to move them. Payout shape, horizon and monitoring determine which gaming strategies are attractive.

lessons.title: Norms, Reciprocity, Status and Safety: The Social Economy of Work
lessons.summary: Much of what people do at work is governed not by formal incentives but by norms, reciprocity, judgments of fairness, identity and the perceived safety of speaking up — forces that formal incentives can strengthen or destroy.
objectives: Explain conditional cooperation and reciprocity, and why cooperation in groups tends to decay without sanctions.
Analyze how fairness judgments depend on reference points and on perceived intentions, not only on amounts.
Evaluate the evidence on psychological safety, distinguishing what is correlational from what is causal.
Predict how a formal incentive might interact with an existing norm, identity or status order.
lessons.executive: Contracts and bonuses cover a small part of what organizations need from people. The rest — helping colleagues, raising problems, going beyond the job description — is sustained by norms, reciprocity, fairness and identity. Experimental economics shows that many people are conditional cooperators: they reciprocate generosity and punish free riding, and group cooperation tends to unravel when free riders cannot be sanctioned. Fairness is judged against reference points and intentions, so the same raise can feel generous or insulting. Psychological safety is associated with learning and performance, but most of that evidence is correlational. Design formal incentives so they reinforce the social economy rather than replace it.

explore.text: Hypothetical: two regional offices of a consulting firm receive identical 4 percent raises in the same year. In the first, people are pleased; the previous year brought no raise, and partners explained the constraints openly. In the second, morale collapses; staff learned through a leaked spreadsheet that a newly hired peer group was given 9 percent, and no partner had mentioned it. The money is the same. The reaction differs because people judged the raise against different reference points and inferred different intentions.
Before reading on: list two things, other than the size of a pay increase, that you think determine whether people experience it as fair. Rank them by how much they would matter to you.

Lessons 2 and 3 treated individuals and their incentives. This lesson turns to the social economy of work: the unwritten exchanges, expectations and status orders that determine whether people cooperate, share information and admit mistakes. Formal incentives sit on top of this economy. Sometimes they reinforce it; sometimes, as the day-care fine showed, they replace a norm with a price.

understand.text: Reciprocity and conditional cooperation

Fehr and Gächter review experimental evidence that a substantial share of people are *reciprocal*: they respond to kindness with kindness and to unkindness with retaliation, even when doing so is costly and brings no future benefit. In gift-exchange experiments, employers who offered more generous wages were on average met with higher effort, although effort was not enforceable. Reciprocity helps make incomplete contracts work: when no contract can specify everything, goodwill fills the gaps.

Reciprocal people coexist with selfish ones, and the mix determines what happens in groups. In public-goods experiments, where each member can contribute to a shared pool that benefits everyone, cooperation typically starts at moderate levels and declines over repeated rounds as conditional cooperators see others free ride and withdraw. When participants can pay to punish free riders, many do, and cooperation can be sustained at much higher levels. The lesson for leaders is that a small number of visible free riders can unravel cooperation among people who were willing to contribute.

understand.title: Prerequisite: the public-goods game and the free-rider problem

blocks.text: In a public-goods game, each member of a small group receives an endowment and decides how much to put into a shared pool. The pool is multiplied and divided equally among all members, whatever they contributed. The group as a whole is best off if everyone contributes everything, but each individual is better off keeping their own endowment while others contribute. That gap between individual and collective interest is the *free-rider problem*. It describes many workplace situations: sharing knowledge, covering for a colleague, mentoring, keeping shared systems tidy. Everyone benefits when these happen, and each person is tempted to let others do them.

understand.caption: Stylized pattern of contributions in repeated public-goods games
understand.note: Synthetic, stylized values chosen to illustrate the qualitative pattern described in R-fehr-2000-fairness (decline without sanctions; sustained or rising cooperation with sanctions). Not data from any study.

understand.text: Norms and the meaning of a transaction

A *social norm* is a shared expectation about what people do and what they ought to do, enforced by approval and disapproval rather than by law. Norms are powerful precisely because they are informal; that is also what makes them fragile. Gneezy and colleagues’ discussion of the day-care fine illustrates the fragility: a price can convert a moral obligation into a market transaction, and the obligation may not return when the price is removed. The same mechanism appears when an organization starts paying for behavior that people previously did as a matter of professional identity.

Norms spread partly through the conformity mechanisms described in Lesson 1. People infer what is appropriate from what others visibly do, especially when they want to belong to the group. Meta-analytic evidence on Asch-type tasks shows conformity is real and larger with larger unanimous majorities, which suggests why a norm, once widespread, is hard for any individual to break.
Fairness, reference points and status

People judge outcomes relative to *reference points*: what they received before, what peers receive, what they were led to expect. A raise below a peer’s can feel like a loss even if it is a gain in absolute terms. Fairness judgments also depend on *intentions*: Fehr and Gächter emphasize that people respond to the perceived kindness or hostility behind an action, not only to its consequences. Two practical corollaries follow. Transparency about the reasons for differences matters as much as the differences themselves, and an action read as distrust (heavy monitoring, a clawback threat) can lower the goodwill it was meant to protect.

*Status* — relative standing in the eyes of others — is a reward that organizations allocate constantly through titles, seating, who is consulted, whose name is on the report. *Social identity* — the part of a person’s self-concept that comes from group membership — makes people care about their group’s standing and its norms. Both are central to how professionals experience their work, and both can be used as incentives that cost no cash. They can also produce in-group favoritism and rivalry between departments. This week treats them as working lenses rather than as findings with precise effect sizes, and does not cite primary studies on them; read claims about their size with that in mind.

understand.text: Psychological safety and its evidence

Psychological safety is a shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks — to ask a question, admit an error or challenge a plan — without being punished or humiliated. Frazier and colleagues’ meta-analysis found psychological safety associated with information sharing, learning behavior, engagement and task performance, and associated with supportive leadership, peer support and work design. The construct has been studied at individual, team and organizational levels.

challenge.text: The popular claim that “psychological safety drives team performance” outruns the evidence. Most primary studies in the meta-analysis are cross-sectional and many rely on the same people reporting both safety and outcomes, which inflates correlations and leaves causal direction open: successful teams may feel safer because they are succeeding. Experimental and longitudinal tests are fewer. Meanwhile, the gift-exchange evidence on reciprocity also shows that laboratory effects can shrink in the field. Both literatures support a direction — candor and goodwill help — without supporting confident promises about how much a program will raise performance.

Psychological safety is also sometimes confused with comfort or low standards. The construct concerns whether candor is punished, not whether expectations are demanding. A team can hold very high standards and still make it safe to report a mistake; arguably high standards make such reporting more necessary. Leaders who hear “psychological safety” as “avoid hard feedback” misapply it.

Finally, norms cut both ways. Strong norms sustain cooperation, but they also sustain bad practices: concealment, hazing, or a refusal to adopt better methods. Conformity and identity make it costly for any one person to break a harmful norm. Changing a norm usually requires visible behavior by high-status members, a credible signal that the old norm will no longer be rewarded, and patience. Weeks 6 and 12 develop the politics and mechanics of that change.

challenge.title: Methodological note: measuring a group-level construct

blocks.text: Psychological safety is conceptualized as a property of a team, but it is measured by asking individuals. Researchers therefore check whether team members agree enough to justify averaging their answers, and they analyze data at the right level. Common pitfalls include treating individual-level correlations as team-level effects, measuring safety and performance from the same survey, and ignoring that teams with good leaders differ in many ways at once. When you read a claim about safety, ask: who rated the outcome, was it measured later than safety, and was anything manipulated?

apply.text: Hypothetical: an air ambulance operator wants crews to report near-misses. Reports are rare. A situational diagnosis finds that the last pilot who reported a near-miss was grounded pending review, and that reports go to the same manager who writes performance appraisals. Remedies follow from this lesson: separate reporting from appraisal, make the response to a report visibly non-punitive for honest errors, have senior captains report their own near-misses first, and close the loop by showing what changed. Paying a bonus per report would risk pricing a professional norm and inviting trivial reports.

Hypothetical: a professional rugby club introduces individual bonuses for tackles made. Tackle counts rise, but some players start chasing tackles out of position, and the defensive system suffers. The reciprocity and norm lens adds a second cost: team-mates who held their positions see others rewarded for undermining the structure, and their willingness to do unglamorous work erodes. A redesign might reward defensive outcomes at team level and use coaches’ judgment to recognize positional discipline.

In player development, norms, status and safety shape how quickly problems surface. A young player who conceals a minor injury or a coach who hides that a drill is not working is responding to the social economy: what happened to the last person who spoke up, whose opinion carries status, and whether candor is treated as weakness. Leaders can change those signals at little cost — by asking questions first, publicly crediting people who surface problems early, and keeping development conversations separate from evaluation where possible. Bilingual and cross-cultural settings add reference-point and identity questions: what counts as respectful disagreement, and whose norms are treated as the default.

apply.title: Executive twist: a fairness complaint with partial information

blocks.text: A respected senior employee tells you privately that a peer is being paid more for the same role, and that “people are talking.” You know the pay difference exists and that it reflects a market premium at the time of hiring. You cannot share individual pay. Ignoring the complaint risks a slow erosion of reciprocity; explaining the specific case breaches confidentiality; equalizing pay immediately is expensive and sets a precedent. A defensible path is to explain the principles behind pay differences in general, commit to a review of the role’s range on a set date, and give the employee voice in that process. You will not know for months whether trust recovered.

retain.text: Much of what organizations need from people is sustained by reciprocity, norms, fairness, status and the safety of speaking up. Many people cooperate conditionally, so visible free riding unravels cooperation unless it is addressed. Fairness is judged against reference points and intentions. Psychological safety is associated with learning and performance, but most evidence is correlational. Formal incentives should be designed to reinforce, not replace, the social economy.

exercise.title: Incentive Designer

intro.text: You are the newly appointed director of patient-care operations at Linden Ferry Medical Center, a fictional mid-sized hospital. Unit 5 West, a 30-bed medical-surgical unit, has three problems leadership wants fixed: late-day discharges that back up the emergency department, a rising rate of patient falls, and mediocre patient-experience scores. The board has approved a modest incentive budget. Your job is to design the incentive system.

Choose one option on each of six dimensions: what is measured, whose performance counts, the time horizon, the payout shape, how performance is monitored, and which non-financial levers you use. The engine totals each option’s effects on six indicators and fires warnings for risky combinations. Try at least three designs: one that maximizes effort on the measured work, one that minimizes gaming, and one you would actually defend to the unit’s nurses. Notice which indicators move together and which trade off.

Every effect is an ordinal teaching heuristic grounded in this week’s readings, shown in words, not a prediction of what would happen in a real hospital. Open “Show the rules” at any time to see every number.

brief.text: Unit 5 West (fictional): 30 beds; about 60 nursing staff across shifts, plus nursing assistants, a unit clerk and a nurse manager. Discharges are often delayed by pharmacy, transport and physician sign-off, not only by nursing. Falls are rare events, so monthly counts are noisy. Patient-experience surveys have low response rates. Staff turnover is moderate, and a neighboring hospital is recruiting. Many nurses describe their motivation in terms of patient care and professional pride. All details are synthetic.

dimensions.label: What is rewarded
dimensions.help: The proxy that pay or recognition is attached to.

options.label: Share of discharges completed before noon
options.why: A precise, easily moved measure; part of it depends on other departments, and the cheapest ways to move it include discharging patients before they are ready or delaying admissions paperwork.

options.label: Patient-experience survey score
options.why: Valued by patients, but low response rates make it noisy, and staff can influence who is surveyed and how questions are framed.

options.label: Audited composite: timely discharge, falls, readmissions and chart quality
options.why: Covering several tasks reduces effort diversion predicted by the multitask model, at the cost of complexity and audit expense.

options.label: No formula: nurse manager’s structured judgment
options.why: Judgment can weigh unmeasured work, but it is open to favoritism and perceived unfairness unless criteria are explicit.

dimensions.label: Whose performance counts
dimensions.help: Individual, team, a mix, or rank among peers.

options.label: Individual nurse
options.why: Sharpens individual effort on attributable tasks, but discharges and fall prevention are team products; individual pay discourages helping.

options.label: Whole unit
options.why: Rewards cooperation and shared work; conditional cooperators may withdraw if free riding is visible and unaddressed.

options.label: Mostly unit, small individual component
options.why: Balances shared outcomes with some individual accountability; more complex to explain.

options.label: Ranking nurses against each other (top quartile paid)
options.why: Tournaments raise effort but turn colleagues into rivals; incentives read as distrust can erode reciprocity.

dimensions.label: Time horizon
dimensions.help: How often performance is measured and paid.

options.label: Monthly
options.why: Frequent feedback, but rare events like falls are mostly noise at monthly scale, and short horizons reward quick fixes.

options.label: Quarterly
options.why: A common compromise between feedback and noise.

options.label: Annual, with part deferred
options.why: Longer horizons average out noise and reduce timing games, but weaken the link between effort and reward.

dimensions.label: Payout shape
dimensions.help: How pay changes as the measure changes.

options.label: Linear: pay per point of improvement
options.why: Constant marginal incentive everywhere; highest power and cost.

options.label: Threshold: fixed bonus only if target met
options.why: Strong incentive only near the target; invites shifting results across periods and giving up when the target is out of reach.

options.label: Linear up to a cap
options.why: Limits extreme behavior and cost, but removes incentives above the cap.

options.label: No cash: recognition and resources only
options.why: Avoids pricing professional norms; weaker direct effect on volume tasks.

options.label: Unit self-reports its numbers
options.why: Signals trust and costs little, but makes cheap manipulation of the measure easy.

options.label: Random audits of a sample of records
options.why: Raises the cost of gaming without signalling blanket distrust.

options.label: Continuous electronic tracking of individual activity
options.why: Reduces some gaming but signals distrust and can crowd out reciprocity and professional pride.

options.label: Manager judgment informed by peer review
options.why: Uses local knowledge of unmeasured work; vulnerable to bias without clear criteria.

options.label: None
options.why: Leaves the social economy as it is.

options.label: Public leaderboard of individual scores
options.why: Adds status competition to the measured task; can feel controlling.

options.label: Peer-nominated recognition for safety catches and help
options.why: Informational recognition supports competence and relatedness and rewards hard-to-measure behavior.

options.label: Unit-led improvement projects with protected time
options.why: Supports autonomy and competence; costs staff time.

rules.text: Monthly pay on before-noon discharges is the classic recipe for discharging patients early or reclassifying discharge times. Watch readmissions and the timestamp process.
A ranking plus a public leaderboard makes colleagues rivals twice over. Expect less help across shifts and possible hoarding of easy patients.
Self-reported survey administration lets the unit choose which patients are surveyed. The score may rise without any change in care.
Monthly thresholds invite moving results across the month boundary and giving up mid-month when the target looks lost.
Team pay without any check on contributions relies entirely on peers to sanction free riding. Conditional cooperators may withdraw if a few people visibly coast.
Protected time for unit-led projects signals autonomy; continuous tracking signals distrust. Staff will notice the mixed message.
Judgment-based reward can capture unmeasured work, but only if criteria are published and decisions explained; otherwise fairness concerns will dominate.
A broad, audited measure over a long horizon is close to what the multitask model recommends for complex jobs. The price is weaker short-term effort and higher administration.
With no cash and no non-financial levers, this design changes little. That may be the right answer if the current problem is mostly caused by other departments.

config.disclaimer: Effects are ordinal teaching heuristics drawn from the cited research, not predictions of behavior in any real hospital. Linden Ferry Medical Center and all details are fictional.

debrief.text: Most learners discover three trade-offs. First, effort on the measured work and gaming risk tend to rise together: the stronger the incentive on a proxy, the more attractive cheap ways of moving it become. Second, individual and ranking schemes raise measured effort at the expense of cooperation, which matters in a unit where discharges and fall prevention are team products. Third, heavy monitoring reduces gaming but can damage intrinsic motivation and reciprocity; audits reduce gaming with less signal of distrust.

There is no best design. A unit-level, audited composite over a longer horizon, combined with recognition for safety catches, scores well on gaming and cooperation but weakly on immediate effort and costs more to administer. Whether that is right depends on facts the exercise cannot show: how much of the discharge delay is under nursing control, how staff interpret incentives, and how the neighboring hospital is recruiting.

What the exercise does not show: actual magnitudes, interactions beyond the listed rules, selection effects (who joins or leaves under each design), or how the design would be implemented and explained. Those questions are where executive judgment, piloting and measurement come in.

assumptions: Effects are ordinal (−3 to +3 per option) and simply add; real effects interact in many more ways than the listed rules capture.
Each option’s effect is a teaching heuristic drawn from the cited literature, not an estimate from hospital data.
Discharge timing depends partly on other departments; the unit cannot fully control it.
Falls are rare events, so short-horizon fall counts are dominated by noise.
Linden Ferry Medical Center, Unit 5 West and all details are fictional.

case.title: The Activation Accelerator
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Lanternfish Payments is an invented company; any resemblance to a real firm is coincidental.

body.text: At 7:40 on a Tuesday morning, Nadia Ferreira-Holt, chief operating officer of Lanternfish Payments, opened a message from the company’s chief risk officer with the subject line “Need 30 minutes before the board deck goes out.” Lanternfish sold a bundle of payments, payroll and expense cards to small businesses — restaurants, contractors, clinics, independent retailers. It had grown quickly for six years, and in ten weeks it would ask investors for its largest funding round yet. The draft board deck, already circulating, led with a single chart: new-account activations up 61 percent in two quarters.

The chart was the product of the Activation Accelerator, a program Nadia had approved nine months earlier. Lanternfish’s account executives had always been paid a salary plus a commission on signed contracts. The problem, as the sales leadership saw it, was that many signed businesses never actually used the product. A customer who signed but never ran a payroll or swiped a card generated no revenue and usually left within a year. So the Accelerator shifted pay. Commission on signatures was halved; in its place, account executives received a bonus of $400 for each new account that “activated” within 30 days of signing. Activation was defined, for simplicity, as the first successful card transaction of any amount or the first payroll run.

The design had been debated. Mateo Varga, vice president of sales, had argued for it forcefully: “We are paying people to sign customers who never use us. Pay them for the thing that predicts revenue.” Theo Brandt, the chief financial officer, liked that the bonus was tied to a behavioral event rather than a promise. A data scientist on Theo’s team had shown that, historically, accounts that activated within 30 days were far more likely to still be active a year later. Nobody had asked whether that relationship would hold once people were paid on it.

The early results looked excellent. Activations rose sharply, and the share of signed accounts that activated within 30 days climbed from about half to more than four in five. The sales team’s morale was high; several account executives earned the largest bonuses in the company’s history. Mateo had been invited to speak about the program at an industry conference.

The message from Ines Calloway, the chief risk officer, described a different picture. Her team had been reviewing first transactions for a fraud-model update and had noticed clusters. Across the last two quarters, 214 new accounts had activated with a single transaction of exactly $1.00. In 37 of them, the transaction originated from devices or networks associated with Lanternfish’s own offices. Nineteen of those 37 accounts belonged to the portfolio of one account executive, a top performer named Corey Lindqvist. The remainder were spread across eleven people. Ines had not yet spoken to anyone in sales.

There was more, and it was less clear-cut. Ninety-day retention of new accounts — the share still transacting three months after signing — had fallen from 58 percent to 46 percent over the same period, even as 30-day activation soared. Customer-support tickets from new accounts complaining about features they “did not know they had signed up for” had roughly doubled. A product manager suggested an innocent explanation for part of this: the Accelerator had brought in a wave of smaller businesses that churn more anyway. Nobody had yet separated the two effects.

Nadia called the four executives together that afternoon. Ines spoke first. “At minimum we have a control failure. At worst we have employees making transactions on customers’ accounts without authorization, which is a regulatory problem, not a sales problem. I want the bonus suspended today, the 37 accounts investigated, and a clawback on any bonus paid for an activation we cannot verify.”

Mateo pushed back. “Thirty-seven accounts out of thousands. Nineteen are one person. I am not going to tell 140 account executives they are under suspicion because of one bad actor and a few people who probably helped a customer test a card in the office — which, by the way, we used to encourage. If we suspend the bonus ten weeks before the raise, half my top performers will be interviewing at competitors by Friday. The program works. Retention is down because we are signing smaller customers, which is the strategy.”

Theo was quieter. He was worried about the board deck. The activation chart was the strongest evidence that Lanternfish’s growth was real rather than purchased. If the company disclosed that the metric was compromised, investors would discount every other number in the deck. If it did not, and the story emerged later, the damage would be worse. “I need to know,” he said, “whether the activation numbers are mostly real with some noise, or mostly noise with some real. I don’t think anyone in this room knows.”

Nadia also had a conversation she had not shared. A week earlier, a senior account executive with a long, clean record had told her privately that the team had a phrase — “a dollar to launch” — and that new hires learned it in their first month. He had not said whether he did it. He had said he was tired of being compared on a leaderboard with people who did.

Nadia did not know how many of the 214 $1.00 activations were legitimate customer tests, how many were employees helping customers in good faith, and how many were employees activating accounts without customer knowledge. She did not know whether the fall in retention reflected gaming, a shift in the customer mix, or both. She did not know whether a public suspension would lead to resignations or whether most of the sales team would quietly welcome a clean reset. And she did not know whether the original data scientist’s finding — that early activation predicts retention — had ever reflected a causal relationship, or whether it simply identified customers who already intended to use the product.

She did know three things. The board deck would go to directors in six days. Any decision she made would be read by 140 account executives as a statement about whether the company trusted them. And whatever replaced the Accelerator would also be gamed by somebody, somehow, unless it was designed with that in mind.

At 6:15 that evening she opened a blank document and typed the heading: “Activation Accelerator — decision and redesign.” Then she stopped, because she was not sure whether the first section should be about the program, the people or the board.

The historical correlation between early activation and retention was measured before anyone was paid on activation.
The customer mix shifted toward smaller businesses after launch, but the size of that shift has not been measured.
