questions: Using the multitask model and Kerr’s diagnostic question, explain how the Accelerator’s design made a $1.00 activation an attractive strategy. Which features of the pay structure mattered most?

What should Nadia do in the next six days about the board deck, the 37 accounts and the bonus? Defend a position that a skeptical board member and a skeptical account executive could both accept as fair.
How would you separate the effect of gaming from the effect of the shifting customer mix on 90-day retention? What data would you need, and what would change your recommendation?
Design a replacement incentive. What is measured, over what horizon, with what payout shape and verification? What new form of gaming should Nadia expect, and how will she detect it?
What signals — about trust, fairness and the company’s norms — will 140 account executives read into each option, and how should that shape the way the decision is communicated?

perspectives.title: Suspend now, investigate, claw back
perspectives.text: The integrity of a financial metric and possible unauthorized activity on customer accounts outweigh short-term sales disruption. Suspend the activation bonus immediately, investigate the 37 accounts with risk and legal involvement, disclose to the board that the metric is under review, and introduce clawbacks for unverified activations. The cost is morale and possibly some departures; the benefit is that the company’s numbers, and its account executives, can be trusted again. This view treats the board deck as secondary to getting the facts right.

perspectives.title: Targeted investigation, redesign without public suspension
perspectives.text: Most activations are probably real, and a blanket suspension tells honest employees they are suspects. Investigate the 37 accounts and the individual with 19 of them quietly and promptly; change the definition of activation going forward (for example, a minimum transaction value, multiple transactions or a payroll run, verified as customer-initiated); remove the leaderboard; disclose to the board that the metric is being tightened and why. The risk is that the problem is wider than it looks and the company is later seen to have moved too slowly.

perspectives.title: Replace the measure, not just the rules
perspectives.text: The core mistake was paying on a single early event because it historically correlated with retention. Any single-event activation measure will decay under pay pressure. Replace the activation bonus with a smaller, deferred bonus based on 90- or 180-day revenue from the account, with team-level components to reduce rivalry, and present the board with retention and revenue alongside activation. This sacrifices immediacy and simplicity, and may reduce effort on signing new customers, but aligns the measure with the goal.

case.application: The structure of this case — a measure that predicted the goal until people were paid on it, a top performer whose results look too good, a leaderboard that turned colleagues into rivals, and a leader who must act before the facts are clear — transfers directly to player development and baseball operations. A development staff paid or promoted on how many players reach a level, or a scouting group judged on short-term statistical markers, faces the same decay of a once-informative measure. The same choices also recur: whether to suspend, investigate or redesign; how to protect people who did nothing wrong; and how to present uncertain numbers to ownership without overstating or hiding the problem.

questions.prompt: Across four regional offices of a hypothetical insurer, new hires in the claims role quit at twice the rate of new hires in other roles. Which inference is best supported before any further investigation?

options.text: The claims role attracts people with weaker commitment.
Something about the claims role — workload, measures, supervision or norms — is a likely contributor and should be examined first.
The recruiters hiring for claims are poor judges of character.
Turnover is random and nothing can be inferred.

questions.explanation: A pattern that recurs across many different people and offices in the same role is evidence about the role. Dispositional explanations are possible but should be tested after situational features shared by all those people are examined.

optionFeedback.a: This jumps to a dispositional explanation for a pattern that shared situational features explain more economically.
optionFeedback.c: Possible, but it is still a person-centred explanation that skips the shared role features.
optionFeedback.d: A consistent doubling across four offices is unlikely to be pure noise.

stimulus.text: Fictional summary: An influential 2009 study (n = 40) reported that employees who first completed a tedious form persisted 40 percent less on a later puzzle. A 2024 preregistered replication across 18 laboratories (total n = 2,300) using the original materials found a difference of 2 percent, with a confidence interval spanning zero.

options.text: The original authors must have fabricated their data.
The original effect was probably inflated or absent; the preregistered multi-lab estimate is far more credible for practical decisions.
The two studies cancel out, so the true effect is about 21 percent.
The replication failed because laboratories differ; the original finding stands.

questions.explanation: A small study with a large reported effect is the profile of an inflated estimate; a large preregistered multi-lab test removes most analytic flexibility and estimates the effect precisely. Inflation does not require fraud, and averaging a tiny study with a huge one is not how evidence should be combined.

optionFeedback.a: Small samples, flexible analysis and publication filters can inflate effects without any misconduct.
optionFeedback.c: Studies should be weighted by precision; the multi-lab estimate dominates.
optionFeedback.d: Lab differences were part of the design and the pooled estimate is still near zero; the objection would need specific, testable conditions.

questions.prompt: Select every statement that is supported by this week’s evidence on motivation.

options.text: Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing an interesting task tend to reduce later free-choice engagement in experiments.
Any payment for work destroys intrinsic motivation.
Intrinsic motivation remained a predictor of performance when incentives were present.
Positive verbal feedback tends to enhance intrinsic motivation.
Self-determination theory treats all extrinsic motivation as equally controlled.
Incentives were associated more with quantity of performance than with quality.

questions.explanation: The undermining effect is conditional on reward type and contingency; verbal feedback tends to help. The forty-year meta-analysis found intrinsic motivation remained predictive alongside incentives, with incentives more related to quantity. Self-determination theory explicitly distinguishes forms of extrinsic motivation, some of which are autonomous.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of the proposal, and the best alternative?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: at a public library system, experienced librarians have for years voluntarily mentored new staff. The director proposes paying $50 per completed mentoring session to “show we value it.”

options.text: No risk; paying for valued behavior always increases it.

Payment may reframe mentoring from professional contribution to a low-paid task and crowd out voluntary effort; recognition, protected time and a mentoring role in promotion criteria are lower-risk ways to show value.
The payment is too large and should be reduced to $10.
Mentoring should be made mandatory instead.

questions.explanation: Small payments for behavior sustained by professional norms risk replacing the norm with a price, as in the day-care example, and can signal that the task is unpleasant. Recognition and resources that support competence and relatedness show value without pricing the behavior.

optionFeedback.a: The crowding-out evidence shows payment does not always increase the paid behavior.
optionFeedback.c: A smaller payment does not avoid reframing and may make the task look less valued.
optionFeedback.d: Mandating it converts autonomous motivation into controlled motivation, the opposite of the goal.

questions.prompt: A salesperson has closed 92 units with ten days left in the quarter. The plan pays a $50 commission per unit plus a one-time $8,000 bonus if the quarter reaches 100 units. If she can pull exactly 8 units forward from next quarter, what is her average payoff per pulled-forward unit from the threshold bonus alone, in dollars? (Ignore the commission, which she earns in either quarter.)
questions.working: The bonus is earned only if she reaches 100. Pulling 8 units forward moves her from 92 to 100 and earns the $8,000 bonus. $8,000 ÷ 8 units = $1,000 per unit — twenty times the $50 commission. This is why thresholds create intense timing incentives near the cliff.
questions.explanation: Near the threshold, each unit moved across the quarter boundary is worth $8,000 divided by the 8 units needed, or $1,000, compared with $50 in commission. Threshold payout shapes concentrate incentive intensity near the target and invite timing games.

questions.prompt: You lead a team of software engineers. A new bonus on story points delivered per sprint has raised throughput by a third, but defect reports from customers are up and senior engineers have stopped reviewing others’ code. With a limited budget and a board that likes the throughput number, what is the best next move?

options.text: Raise the story-point bonus so that engineers can afford to spend time on reviews.
Keep the bonus but add a defect-rate penalty applied to each individual engineer.
Reduce the power of the story-point bonus, move part of it to a team-level measure that includes escaped defects, and protect code review in role expectations.
Abolish all incentives and return to the previous system without explanation.

questions.explanation: The multitask model predicts effort diversion from unmeasured tasks (review, quality) toward the paid one. Weakening the incentive on the narrow measure, broadening it at team level to include quality, and protecting review in the job design addresses the diversion without abandoning accountability.

optionFeedback.a: A stronger incentive on story points increases diversion away from unmeasured work.
optionFeedback.b: Individual defect penalties discourage taking on hard work and helping others, and invite hiding defects.
optionFeedback.d: Abolishing incentives silently forfeits the throughput gain and gives the board and team no rationale.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical regional bank pays branch staff a monthly bonus per new account opened, with self-reported data and a public leaderboard. Rank these redesigns from most to least likely to reduce unauthorized account openings while keeping a sales incentive.

options.text: Pay on accounts still active and funded after 90 days, verified by random audits, with the leaderboard removed.
Keep the per-account bonus but add a code-of-conduct training module.
Keep everything but double the number of accounts required for the bonus.
Pay on new accounts opened, but require a customer signature captured electronically.

questions.explanation: Paying on verified, durable outcomes with audits and no rivalry addresses the measure, the horizon and monitoring together. Requiring a verified customer signature closes the cheapest fabrication route but keeps a volume measure. Training changes nothing structural. Raising the target intensifies pressure on the same gameable measure and likely makes things worse.

questions.prompt: Identify the main flaw in this reasoning.

stimulus.text: Consultant’s slide: “Teams in the top quartile of psychological safety had 30 percent higher performance ratings from their own members. Therefore our psychological-safety workshop will raise your performance by 30 percent.”

options.text: It treats a cross-sectional, self-rated association as the causal effect of an intervention, and assumes the workshop changes safety by a full quartile.
Psychological safety has never been studied.
The comparison should have used the bottom quartile only.
Thirty percent is too small to matter.

questions.explanation: Same-source ratings inflate associations, performance may cause felt safety, and nothing shows the workshop changes safety, let alone by the amount separating quartiles. The meta-analytic evidence supports an association, not a causal effect of this size.

optionFeedback.b: Psychological safety has a sizeable literature, including a meta-analysis.
optionFeedback.c: Changing the comparison group does not fix the causal leap.
optionFeedback.d: The size is not the problem; the inference is.

questions.prompt: Two hospital departments receive the same 3 percent raise. Department A had been told raises would be frozen; Department B learned afterwards that a newly hired group received 8 percent. According to this week’s material, why might B react much worse?

options.text: B’s staff are more materialistic.
Fairness is judged against reference points and inferred intentions; B’s reference point is the new hires’ raise and the undisclosed difference may be read as disrespect.
The raise in B is objectively smaller.
People only care about absolute pay, so the reactions should be identical.

questions.explanation: The same amount is compared with different reference points — a freeze in A, a peer’s larger raise in B — and the way B learned of the difference invites an inference about intentions. Reciprocity responds to perceived kindness or unkindness, not only to amounts.

optionFeedback.a: A dispositional explanation ignores the different situations the two departments are in.
optionFeedback.c: The raises are identical in size.
optionFeedback.d: This contradicts the evidence that fairness judgments are relative and intention-sensitive.

questions.prompt: A team’s willingness to do unglamorous shared work has declined. Select every change that this week’s evidence suggests could help.

options.text: Address visible free riding promptly and consistently.
Introduce a public individual leaderboard on the shared work.
Have senior, high-status members visibly do the shared work.
Recognize contributions to shared work in ways peers can see and endorse.
Announce that anyone not contributing will be monitored by continuous tracking.
Ignore it; norms always recover on their own.

questions.explanation: Conditional cooperators withdraw when free riding goes unaddressed, so addressing it matters. Norms spread through visible behavior by high-status members, and informational, peer-endorsed recognition supports competence and relatedness. Leaderboards add rivalry; blanket surveillance signals distrust; norms that have begun to unravel do not reliably recover unaided.

questions.prompt: A hypothetical public school district plans to pay teachers a bonus based on the share of students passing a standardized test each spring. In 150–250 words, predict two intended and two unintended consequences, using at least two concepts from different lessons this week, and propose one design change that reduces an unintended consequence while keeping some accountability.
questions.modelAnswer: Intended: teachers will spend more effort on tested skills and on students near the passing line, and weak instruction in tested subjects may become visible. Unintended (multitask): effort will move away from untested subjects, deeper projects and students far above or below the passing threshold, because the measure pays only for crossing a line — a threshold payout shape. Unintended (gaming): some schools may narrow who sits the test or teach test formats rather than skills, so the pass rate decays as a measure of learning. A further risk (crowding out and reciprocity) is that teachers who see themselves as professionals may read individual pay on a single test as distrust, weakening voluntary effort such as mentoring colleagues. Design change: base a smaller, school-level bonus on growth across the full score distribution over two years, audited for test participation, combined with peer-reviewed professional goals. This keeps accountability while reducing the threshold incentive and the rivalry and distrust signals of individual pay.

rubric.criterion: Predicts intended and unintended consequences with mechanisms
levels: 2 — two intended and two unintended consequences, each tied to a mechanism

rubric.criterion: Uses concepts from at least two lessons correctly
levels: 2 — concepts from two or more lessons used correctly

rubric.criterion: Proposes a design change that targets a named side effect and keeps accountability
levels: 1 — change proposed but not linked to a side effect
2 — targeted change with its own likely trade-off noted

reserve.prompt: You chair a panel deciding which of five vendors to select. Given the conformity evidence, which procedure best protects independent judgment?

options.text: The most senior member states a view first to give the group direction.
Members submit written rankings independently before discussion; the chair speaks last.
Discuss openly and vote by show of hands.
Let the vendor with the most enthusiastic supporter win.

reserve.explanation: Conformity pressure is strongest when people hear a majority or high-status view before forming their own. Independent written judgments before discussion, with the chair last, preserve the information each member holds.

optionFeedback.a: A senior first view invites conformity toward it.
optionFeedback.c: Public voting after discussion adds visible conformity pressure.
optionFeedback.d: Enthusiasm is a social signal, not evidence.

reserve.prompt: Which incentive design fits this task best, given the evidence on incentives and intrinsic motivation?

stimulus.text: Hypothetical: a logistics firm needs warehouse staff to scan and shelve a backlog of 40,000 returned items in two weeks. The task is repetitive and staff report little interest in it. Accuracy can be checked automatically by scanner.

options.text: No incentive; intrinsic motivation will carry the work.
A direct per-item incentive with automatic accuracy checks, time-limited to the backlog.
A peer-recognition program only.
A ranking tournament where the bottom quartile loses shifts.

reserve.explanation: For low-interest, volume tasks with cheap quality checks, direct incentives raise quantity with little intrinsic motivation at stake. Automatic accuracy checks limit gaming, and time-limiting avoids converting an ongoing role into piece work.

optionFeedback.a: There is little intrinsic interest to rely on for this task.
optionFeedback.c: Recognition is valuable but weak for a short, repetitive volume push.
optionFeedback.d: Penalizing the bottom quartile adds rivalry and fear without a quality benefit.

reserve.prompt: Why do principals use incentive pay at all, according to agency theory?

options.text: Because agents are dishonest.
Because the principal cannot directly observe the agent’s effort and pays on outcomes correlated with it.
Because incentive pay is always cheaper than salary.
Because incentives eliminate the need for monitoring.

reserve.explanation: Incentive pay is a response to hidden action: when effort is unobservable, paying on correlated outcomes motivates effort. The cost is that pay then depends on noise and on what the measure misses.

optionFeedback.a: The model needs only divergent interests and hidden effort, not dishonesty.
optionFeedback.c: Incentive pay shifts risk to agents, who typically require compensation for bearing it.
optionFeedback.d: Incentives on imperfect measures increase the need to monitor for gaming.

reserve.prompt: Near-miss reports in your clinical laboratory have dropped to almost zero since a technician was disciplined after reporting a sample mix-up. What is the best next move?

options.text: Pay a bonus for each near-miss report.
Separate reporting from performance evaluation, make the response to honest error visibly non-punitive, and have senior staff report their own near-misses first.
Require every technician to file at least two reports per month.
Wait; reporting will recover once people forget the incident.

reserve.explanation: The drop is a predictable response to a punished messenger. Changing the consequences of reporting and having high-status members model the norm addresses the cause. Paying per report or setting quotas invites trivial or fabricated reports.

optionFeedback.a: Paying per report risks pricing a professional norm and inviting low-value reports.
optionFeedback.c: Quotas turn reporting into a gameable count.

assignment.title: Incentive Misalignment Audit: The Mesa Verde Condors

brief.text: The Mesa Verde Condors are a fictional professional baseball organization with a major-league club, several minor-league affiliates, an amateur scouting department, an international program, a player-development staff and a research and analytics group. Use only generic, hypothetical situations; do not draw on confidential information or the practices of any real organization. Invent the specific measures and pay arrangements you analyze, stating them as assumptions.

Your task is to audit the organization’s incentive structure and identify at least three plausible misalignments between groups — for example between amateur scouting and player development, between player development and the major-league coaching staff, or between front-office metrics and what any of these groups are asked to do. For each, explain the mechanism using this week’s concepts, propose a redesign, and predict the side effects of your redesign honestly. A redesign that creates no new problem has not been examined carefully enough.

items: Possible measures to consider (invent and state your own): signing-class outcomes credited to scouts; the number of players promoted or reaching the majors credited to development staff; short-term statistical improvement credited to coaches; win–loss and individual statistics at affiliates; report volume or model adoption credited to analysts; budget adherence credited to department heads.
Possible levers: what is measured, whose performance counts, horizon and deferral, payout shape, monitoring and discretion, status and recognition, decision rights.
Remember the social economy: reciprocity between departments, norms about sharing information, fairness of credit, and whether staff can safely report that something is not working.

brief.text: Write as an internal memo to a fictional general manager. Data, if any, must be labelled synthetic.

assignment.deliverable: A 900–1,400-word memo identifying three incentive misalignments in a fictional baseball organization, with mechanisms, redesigns and predicted side effects.

template.heading: Summary and recommendation
template.guidance: In three to five sentences, state the three misalignments and the single redesign you would prioritize first, and why.

template.heading: Assumed incentive structure
template.guidance: Describe the measures, rewards, horizons and decision rights you are assuming for each group. Make clear these are hypothetical.

template.heading: Misalignment 1–3: mechanism
template.guidance: For each misalignment, describe what is rewarded, what is hoped for, and the mechanism (multitask diversion, gaming, crowding out, free riding, fairness, status). Cite course concepts.

template.heading: Redesigns
template.guidance: For each misalignment, propose a specific change in measure, unit, horizon, payout shape, monitoring or non-financial levers. Explain why it should help.

template.heading: Predicted side effects and how you would detect them
template.guidance: For each redesign, name the most likely new problem (new gaming route, cost, weaker effort, fairness concerns) and the early-warning signal you would watch.

template.heading: Evidence and uncertainty
template.guidance: Distinguish which parts of your reasoning rest on robust evidence, which on theory, and which on your own judgment. Say what information would change your recommendation.

prompts: Recall a time you attributed a colleague’s behavior to their character. What situational feature — measure, norm, status, friction — might have produced the same behavior in most people? What would you do differently now?
Which parts of your own work do you do for intrinsic reasons, and which for external ones? Has any reward, metric or evaluation ever changed how you felt about work you used to enjoy?
Identify one measure in your professional world that you think has started to decay under pressure. Who benefits from it continuing to be used, and what would it cost to replace it?
When did you last see someone in a meeting hold back a dissenting view? What about the situation made dissent costly, and what could the person chairing have changed?

review.front: What does it suggest when the same performance problem recurs across different people in the same role?
review.back: That features of the role or situation — measures, norms, status, friction — are likely contributors and should be examined before individual character.

review.front: Summarize the meta-analytic evidence on conformity in Asch-type tasks.
review.back: Robust but variable: larger with larger majorities and in more collectivist cultures, and declining in U.S. samples over the decades after Asch.

review.front: What did the 2015 Open Science Collaboration find about replication effect sizes?
review.back: Replication effects averaged roughly half the original estimates; far fewer replications than originals were significant, and social psychology replicated less often than cognitive psychology.

review.front: What happened when ego depletion was tested in a preregistered multi-lab replication?
review.back: The pooled effect was close to zero; the popular “willpower runs out” claim lacks reliable support.

review.front: Name the three basic needs proposed by self-determination theory.
Which rewards most reliably undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation in experiments?
review.back: Expected, tangible rewards contingent on doing, completing or performing the task. Verbal positive feedback tended to enhance it; unexpected rewards had little effect.

review.front: What happened after a fine for late pickup was introduced at Israeli day-care centers?
review.back: Late pickups rose and stayed high after the fine was removed — the price replaced a moral obligation.

review.front: According to the forty-year meta-analysis, how do intrinsic motivation and incentives relate to performance?
review.back: They jointly predict it; intrinsic motivation remained predictive with incentives present, relates more to quality, and matters less when incentives are directly tied to performance. Incentives relate more to quantity.

review.front: Why do principals use incentive pay, and what does it cost?
review.back: Effort is unobservable, so they pay on correlated outcomes. The cost: pay depends on luck and on whatever the measure misses.

review.front: State the multitask problem in one sentence.
review.back: Strong incentives on easily measured tasks pull effort from hard-to-measure ones, so weaker incentives or job redesign can be optimal.

review.front: Why does a measure decay once pay depends on it?
review.back: People find cheaper ways to move the measure than to move the goal, so the measure’s correlation with the goal weakens (Goodhart’s and Campbell’s laws).

review.front: What behavior does a threshold (cliff) bonus invite?
review.back: Shifting results across periods near the threshold and easing off when the target is far above or out of reach.

review.front: What happens to cooperation in repeated public-goods games with and without sanctions?
review.back: Without sanctions it typically declines as conditional cooperators withdraw; with the option to punish free riders it can be sustained.

review.front: Why can identical raises feel fair in one unit and unfair in another?
review.back: Fairness is judged against reference points (prior pay, peers, expectations) and inferred intentions, not only amounts.

review.front: What is the main limitation of the evidence that psychological safety improves performance?
review.back: Most studies are cross-sectional and same-source, so causal direction and common-method bias are unresolved.

preview.text: This week’s ideas recur throughout the semester. Motivation reappears in Week 3 as a condition for learning and skill acquisition. The replication record is examined statistically in Week 4. Trust, feedback and psychological safety become leadership practices in Week 5, and status and informal power become organizational politics in Week 6. Principal–agent problems return in Week 7’s negotiation and contracting, and incentive alignment, Goodhart’s law and performance management are the core of Week 8’s organizational design. Week 13 asks who is accountable when systems produce misconduct.
